newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia brings annual inflation to post-reform low.
newsitem.headline: Russia brings annual inflation to post-reform low.

text.p: Russian year-on-year inflation fell below 20 percent last month for the first time since reforms began, but economists said on Friday the good news was partly offset by problems elsewhere in the economy.
The State Statistics Committee said consumer prices rose an 19.7 percent in the year to January, while gross domestic product crept up 0.1 percent.

"This is the best crop of macro-economic statistics we've seen since the second quarter of 1995, the last time industrial output showed any signs of life," said Christopher Granville, head of research at United City Bank.
He said the inflation figures showed the government was on target to meet its 11.8 percent 1997 inflation goal.

But other figures showed 22 percent of the population -- or 31.9 million people -- receiving wages at or below the subsistence level. This is above December's 18 percent but below last January's 25 percent.
The committee said the government's total debt to workers and pensioners rose to 9.48 trillion roubles in January, from 9.28 trillion roubles in December.
Oleg Larichev, economic analyst at Troika Dialog, pointed out that growth figures could well be higher than recorded.
"The government in general doesn't fully take into account the size of the shadow economy, where most of the service sector is, so GDP (growth) could be even higher than 0.1 percent," Larichev said.
But analysts said it was too early to predict whether the slim year-on-year growth figure for January would point to growth over the year as a whole.
The economy has contracted every year since Russia first launched its economic reform programme in January 1992.

"This is the first time there's been a pickup to positive growth but we'll have to see what happens in February," said one Western economist who asked not to be named. "Non-payments and tax arrears still pose significant obstacles to growth."
